blocks.text: The qualifications for overseers and deacons focus on conduct that can be seen and tested: character, speech, self-control, financial integrity, care for a household, and public reputation. The lists present leadership as service requiring maturity and trustworthiness, rather than merely a title or position.

Several expressions in these lists do not settle every later question about church office. “Overseer” and “deacon” may describe roles that should not simply be mapped onto later church structures. Likewise, “husband of one wife” is an idiom whose implications for marriage, remarriage, and eligibility remain disputed. The comparison between household management and care for the community uses an ancient household analogy; it should not be taken to endorse coercive control or abuse.

Verse 11 introduces women with qualifications parallel to those for deacons. The Greek does not include an explicit possessive such as “their,” so the phrase may refer to women deacons, female coworkers, or deacons’ wives. The wording itself does not resolve the question.

The six balanced lines in verse 16 likely preserve rhythmic traditional material: manifestation, vindication, angels, proclamation among the nations, belief in the world, and glory. Its precise origin and structure remain debated, as does a textual question at the opening over whether the subject is read as “who” or “God.”
P133 is a third-century papyrus fragment that preserves part of the transition from the end of this chapter into the next, covering portions of 1 Timothy 3:13-4:8.
